passage: The canteen was loud, the bell was in five minutes, and Sachin was in a rush. "So you're saying you don't want to be group leader? Why not? What's the reason?" he fired at Chandrika. She stiffened and looked at her tray. "I never said that." Sachin realised his voice was sharp. He put his fork down. "Sorry. That sounded like an interrogation. I really want to understand. Do you want to talk at break, when it's quieter?" Chandrika's shoulders lowered. "Yes. I'm not sure myself yet." "Take your time," said Sachin. "I'll wait."

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the bell?
qa.a: The bell was in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Sachin fired his questions?
qa.a: She felt pressured and defensive, since she stiffened and looked at her tray. She also said she wasn't sure herself.

qa.q: What could Sachin do differently next time?
qa.a: He can slow down, use a warmer tone and pick a quieter moment. Probing questions can feel like interrogation when rushed.

qa.q: How might Sachin have seen his own questions?
qa.a: He wanted to understand, but noticed his voice was sharp. He apologised and offered a quieter time.

grounding: A teenager asks confirming and probing questions that feel like interrogation, and softens his tone.

passage: After Imran missed the match, Parveen sat next to him on the wall. "So you're saying you're fine with sitting out? What's behind that?" she asked, warmly, her head tilted. Imran picked at his laces. "My knee felt off. And I didn't want to say." It felt good to be asked. The next day, a senior stopped him in the corridor and said the same thing in a hard voice: "So you're saying you're fine with sitting out? Reason?" Imran felt himself go tense and defensive. The words were nearly the same, but they landed differently.

qa.q: Where did Parveen sit next to Imran?
qa.a: She sat next to him on the wall.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the senior asked him the same question?
qa.a: He felt tense and defensive, since the hard voice made it feel like an interrogation. With Parveen's warmth he felt supported.

qa.q: What could the senior do to make his question feel supportive?
qa.a: Use a warmer tone and show he's on Imran's side. Probing questions depend on tone and relationship.

qa.q: How might Parveen see her questions compared to the senior's?
qa.a: Parveen asked warmly as a friend and it helped him open up. The same words in a hard voice from someone less close can feel like pressure.

grounding: A teenager's confirming and probing questions feel supportive from a friend and like interrogation from a harder voice.

passage:
"Ishita, you're quitting dance?"
"Yeah. I told Ma'am today."
"So you're saying you don't like it anymore?"
"No, I still like it."
"Then why? Is it the new teacher? Is it because of the competition? Did someone say something? Is it your parents?"
Ishita crossed her arms. "Bhupen, this feels like a police interrogation."
Bhupen stopped. "Sorry. I just... I thought I was helping."
"I know. But slow down."
He took a breath. "Okay. One question. Do you want to tell me why?"
Ishita was quiet for a second. "The practices clash with my science tuition. I have to choose."
"That's hard."
"Yeah. Thanks for asking the right way."

qa.q: What clashes with Ishita's dance practice?
qa.a: Her science tuition.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when Bhupen fired questions at her?
qa.a: Ishita felt pressured and annoyed, like she was being interrogated.

qa.q: What did Bhupen change that helped?
qa.a: He slowed down and asked one gentle question, making the probing feel supportive instead of pushy.

qa.q: How did Bhupen see his first rush of questions?
qa.a: Bhupen thought he was helping, not realising his tone felt like interrogation.

grounding: Two teenagers show how probing questions can feel like interrogation or support depending on tone.

passage:
In Class 10, when I told my best friend Sahil I was thinking of dropping science, he didn't just say "okay." He said, "So you're saying you want to drop science because the tuition fees are too high?"
I said, "No, it's more that I don't enjoy it."
He nodded. "Okay, so you're saying you'd rather do commerce because you like it more?"
"Yes. Exactly."
It felt good. Like he was really listening and checking he understood. He didn't try to change my mind. He just asked, "What made you realise that?"
It helped me think it through out loud.
- Jeevan

qa.q: What stream did Jeevan want to switch to?
qa.a: Commerce.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when Sahil checked what Jeevan meant?
qa.a: Jeevan felt listened to and supported, glad Sahil was trying to understand.

qa.q: What made Sahil's questions feel supportive?
qa.a: His calm tone, his checking with "so you're saying," and his not trying to change Jeevan's mind.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt about Jeevan's decision?
qa.a: Sahil seemed accepting and interested, wanting to understand rather than argue.

grounding: The narrator recalls a friend's confirmation questions feeling supportive because of a caring tone.

passage:
Coach's note, Friday
Usha, our team captain, confronted Neha today about missing two practices. "So you're saying you just didn't feel like coming? Why? Were you at the mall? Do you not care about the team?"
Neha went red and stared at the ground. She didn't answer.
I asked Usha to step aside with me. I told her that her questions were fair but her tone felt like an interrogation.
Usha thought about it, then went back and asked more softly, "Is something going on? You don't have to tell me everything."
Neha said her grandmother was unwell and she'd been helping at home.
Usha apologised. They agreed Neha would let her know next time.
- Coach Hansa

qa.q: How many practices had Neha missed?
qa.a: Two practices.

qa.q: What was Neha feeling when Usha fired questions at her?
qa.a: Neha felt embarrassed and cornered, as if being interrogated.

qa.q: What did Coach Hansa do that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out that Usha's tone felt like interrogation, helping Usha ask more gently.

qa.q: How did Usha see her first questions?
qa.a: Usha thought they were fair as captain, not realising her tone made Neha feel attacked.

grounding: A coach's note shows a teenager captain's probing questions feeling like interrogation until she softens her tone.

passage:
Wednesday, late
Told Ira at recess that I'm leaving the quiz team. Ira put her samosa down and started: "So you're saying you're bored of quiz? Or bored of Varun being captain? Why now, two weeks before inter-school? Why didn't you tell Ma'am first?" Four questions in one breath, eyebrows up, like a TV lawyer. I felt cornered and said, "Can I finish one sentence, please?" Ira went quiet and picked at the samosa. On the walk home she tried again, slower: "I asked that badly. I'm not trying to catch you out, Damini. I'll just miss doing the rapid-fire round with you. What's actually going on?" Same kind of question, totally different feeling. So I told her the real thing: Varun laughs every time I get one wrong. She said, "So you're saying it's him, not quiz?" Yes. Exactly that.

qa.q: Where did Ira start asking the questions?
qa.a: Ira started at recess, after putting her samosa down.

qa.q: How did Damini feel when Ira fired four questions at recess?
qa.a: Damini felt cornered and irritated, snapping 'Can I finish one sentence, please?' It may also have been embarrassment about the real reason, Varun laughing.

qa.q: What made the second round of questions work better?
qa.a: Ira slowed down, admitted asking badly, gave the caring reason for asking, and asked one open question, so the probing felt like support instead of a trial.

qa.q: How might Ira have seen the first round of questions?
qa.a: Ira probably meant them as surprise and care about the timing, and was hurt when Damini snapped, going quiet and picking at the samosa.

grounding: It shows 'so you're saying' and probing questions feeling like interrogation at first and like support later, depending on tone and the reason behind them.
